blocks.text: On the dove's feathers, neck, eyes, moaning and flight.

I should like to begin the description of the dove with its plumage and feathers, whose beauty [col. 9] the sacred poet commends thus in Psal. LXVIII, 14. The wings of the dove covered with silver, and its feathers with the paleness of gold. Wings and feathers here stand by συνεκδοχὴν [synekdochēn] for the whole body. Covered with silver, that is, supremely white like silver, and bright with a certain brilliance. For silver is called ἀργύριον [argyrion] in Greek from τὸ ἀργὸν, τὸ λευκόν [to argon, to leukon]; and things that are especially bright are called silver. Hence in the poets ἀργυρόπεζα Θέτις [argyropeza Thetis], that is, λευκόπους [leukopous]. So it is in Hesychius, who likewise explains ἀργυροδίνην κρήνην [argyrodinēn krēnēn] as λευκὰ ῥεύματα ἔχουσαν [leuka rheumata echousan]; and in book 8 of the Aeneid,
is, according to Servius, an epithet of colour. The raven, too, was once a silver bird, when it equalled doves in whiteness. Ovid, Metam. book 2, Fable 7:

For this bird was once silver, with snow-white feathers, so as to equal doves wholly without blemish. [II, 534] For among doves some are exceedingly white ^{(1)}. Varro, De re rustica book 3, ch. 7: The other kind of doves is gentler; content with domestic food, it usually feeds within the threshold of the door. This kind is mostly white in colour. That is, at times and in some places, not always nor everywhere. For in Greece white doves were seen late, namely when the forces of Xerxes were destroyed at Mount Athos. This is expressly reported in the Persica by Charon of Lampsacus, who lived at that time and wrote before Herodotus. Athenaeus, book 9: Χάρων δ᾽ ὁ Λαμψακηνὸς, ἐν τοῖς Περσικοῖς περὶ Μαρδονίου ἱστορῶν, καὶ τοῦ διαφθαρέντος στρατοῦ Περσικοῦ περὶ τὸν Ἄθω, γράφει ταῦτα· „Καὶ λευκαὶ περιστεραὶ τότε πρῶτον εἰς „Ἕλληνας ἐφάνησαν, πρότερον οὐ γιγνόμεναι“. [Charōn d᾽ ho Lampsakēnos, en tois Persikois peri Mardoniou historōn, kai tou diaphtharentos stratou Persikou peri ton Athō, graphei tauta: „Kai leukai peristerai tote prōton eis Hellēnas ephanēsan, proteron ou gignomenai“.] Charon of Lampsacus, treating in the Persica of Mardonius and of the Persian army destroyed at Mount Athos, writes this: „And white doves were then first seen among the Greeks, there having been none before“; that is, in Greece, not anywhere, as the translator there wrongly has it. Aelian in the Varia, book 1, ch. 15: Χάρων δὲ ὁ Λαμψακηνὸς περὶ τὸν Ἄθω φανῆναι περιστερὰς λευκὰς λέγει, ὅτε ἐνταῦθα ἀπώλοντο αἱ τῶν Περσῶν τριέρεις παρακάμπτουσαι τὸν Ἄθω· [Charōn de ho Lampsakēnos peri ton Athō phanēnai peristeras leukas legei, hote entautha apōlonto hai tōn Persōn trierēs parakamptousai ton Athō] But Charon of Lampsacus asserts that white doves were seen around Athos when the triremes of the Persians perished there while sailing past Athos. There follows in the Psalm ואברותיה בירקרק חרוץ, And its feathers with the paleness of gold; supply covered, which is to be repeated from the preceding hemistich. With the paleness of gold, that is, with gold of paleness, or pale gold. Similarly Habac. II, 6. עב טיט, thickness of mud, for mud of thickness, or thick mud: התואר במקום המתואר, the predicate for the subject, as Kimchi has it here. Gold is called חרוץ charuts, that is, dug out of the earth, here and in Zach. IX, 3. and throughout the Proverbs of Solomon ^{(2)}. From this comes the Greek χρυσός [chrysos]. And the paleness of gold is ירקרק, with doubled letters so that the meaning is intensified. Accordingly from this very word comes the Ethiopic ወርቅ፡ vvark for gold. The Greek translators rightly call the paleness of gold χλωρότητα χρυσίου [chlōrotēta chrysiou]. For this is the true colour of gold. Hence Diogenes, asked Διὰ τί τὸ χρυσίον χλωρόν ἐστιν; [Dia ti to chrysion chlōron estin?] Why [II, 535] is gold pale? replied, Ὅτι πολλοὺς ἔχει τοὺς ἐπιβουλεύοντας [Hoti pollous echei tous epibouleuontas], Because it has many who lie in wait for it. So it is in Laertius; and Catullus in the wedding of Peleus and Thetis:
O how often she grew paler than the sallowness of gold!
A guest paler than a gilded statue.
And Statius to Maximus Junius in book 4 of the Silvae:
When will the Dalmatian mountains send you back to sweet Latium, where, having seen Dis, the pale miner returns, the same colour as the gold he has dug up.
